entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Enheduanna, a royal princess of the Akkadian Empire and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, stands as the earliest named author in recorded history, flourishing circa 23rd century BCE. Serving as the High Priestess of Nanna, the moon god, at the temple complex in Ur, she wielded immense religious and political authority, instrumental in consolidating her father's empire by harmonizing Sumerian and Akkadian religious traditions. Her literary output, particularly her hymns and epic poetry, provides an unparalleled window into the spiritual and political landscape of early Mesopotamia, establishing her as a foundational figure in both ancient literature and religious syncretism.

Her principal achievements include composing the 'Exaltation of Inanna' (Nin-me-šar-ra), a 153-line devotional poem to the goddess Inanna, and a collection of 42 'Sumerian Temple Hymns' (En-hedu-an-na-zid-du). These works are not merely religious texts but sophisticated literary pieces that blend theological doctrine with personal reflection and political allegory, showcasing her profound poetic skill and theological insight. As High Priestess, she oversaw the cult of Nanna and significantly influenced the religious practices across Sumer and Akkad, strategically integrating the worship of the Sumerian goddess Inanna with the Semitic Ishtar, thus fostering unity within Sargon's vast, multi-ethnic domain.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Enheduanna is recognized as the earliest named author in world history, whose literary works profoundly influenced Mesopotamian religion and literature for over 500 years, while her political role helped unify the Akkadian Empire.
